claim: Language-model agents can be helpful explainers of already-localized transformer circuits by recovering individual components’ functional roles and the computation implemented by the circuit as a whole. Helpfulness is established if at least one agent correctly classifies more than 50% of circuit components, achieves mean role-description quality above 0.50 on a 0–1 scale where 0, 0.5, and 1 represent incorrect, partially correct, and correct descriptions, and correctly identifies the overall task for more than 50% of circuits. Because the circuit is supplied in advance, the claim concerns explanation after localization rather than circuit discovery.

experiments: Build the controlled circuit-explanation benchmark. Start from the 84 RASP-derived semi-synthetic transformer models in InterpBench, excluding the two IOI tasks to reduce reliance on memorized circuit explanations, and trace each localized trained component through InterpBench’s high-level/low-level correspondence map to the RASP variable it implements. Manually annotate every component with a task-specific note and one of five tags—INDICATOR, AGGREGATOR, ROUTER, MAPPER, or COMBINER—and give each task its RASP program, ground-truth task description, and five input-output examples sampled from the task distribution and produced by executing the program. The resulting AGENTICINTERPBENCH contains 84 circuits and 163 components: 120 MLPs and 43 attention components, with 72 MAPPER, 32 AGGREGATOR, 33 COMBINER, 11 ROUTER, and 15 INDICATOR annotations; circuits contain 1.94 components on average, with a range of 1–10.

Fix the agent workflow and execution budget used for every benchmark run. For each supplied localized component, run HYVE’s observation, hypothesis-generation, and causal-validation loop, withholding the five-class taxonomy until the later classification stage; after processing all components, assign tags and role notes and infer the circuit’s task from the validated component hypotheses and input-output examples. Observation and validation code may use provided TransformerLens helper libraries or custom Python; failed code receives its error message and may be revised for up to five execution attempts per stage. Permit at most three hypothesis-validation iterations per component, retain the latest hypothesis as tentative if none is supported, and measure exact tag accuracy, role-description quality rescaled from judge scores of 0, 1, and 2 to 0, 0.5, and 1, binary task-description accuracy, and the fraction of execute_python calls that run without error.

Validate the LLM-scored explanation metrics against blinded human ratings. Have two human judges independently score anonymized and randomized HYVE outputs using the same role-description and task-description rubrics, and use the lower of their two scores as the human label, matching the lower-score aggregation used for GPT-5.4 and Gemini-3.1-Pro as LLM judges. On the cross-backbone subset of 10 tasks and 17 components, comprising 68 component-level and 40 task-level model-output instances, human-human agreement is κ=0.83 for role-description quality and κ=0.96 for task accuracy; agreement between the lower human score and lower LLM-judge score is κ=0.76 and κ=0.80, respectively. On the larger GPT-5.4/Claude-Sonnet-4.6 annotation set, comprising 110 component-level and 62 task-level instances, human-human agreement is κ=0.802 for role descriptions and κ=0.963 for task accuracy, while lower-human versus lower-LLM agreement is κ=0.753 and κ=0.864. Validation-plan soundness is less reliable: human-human κ is 0.37 on the cross-backbone subset and 0.460 on the larger subset, so the authors retain it as a process diagnostic rather than an official benchmark metric.

Test whether LM agents can explain supplied localized circuits. Run the full HYVE workflow over all 84 AGENTICINTERPBENCH circuits and 163 components with GPT-5.4, Claude-Sonnet-4.6, Gemini-3.1-Pro, and Qwen-3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct. GPT-5.4 obtains tag accuracy 0.74, role-description quality 0.46, task accuracy 0.63, and code-execution success 0.52; Claude-Sonnet-4.6 obtains 0.79, 0.58, 0.75, and 0.93; Gemini-3.1-Pro obtains 0.76, 0.59, 0.83, and 0.80; and Qwen-3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct obtains 0.67, 0.25, 0.25, and 0.62. Claude-Sonnet-4.6 has the highest component-tag accuracy, Gemini-3.1-Pro has the highest judged role-description and task accuracy, and no backbone is best on every metric.

Check whether the generated hypotheses are supported by the agents’ own observations. On the 10-task, 17-component human-validation subset, manually score every observation-hypothesis pair from all four backbones on a 0–2 scale, where 0 means the hypothesis contradicts or ignores the observation, 1 means partial support, and 2 means full support. The three proprietary backbones average 1.94, with one partially supported hypothesis and no ungrounded hypotheses. Qwen-3-Coder averages 1.41 and has fully grounded hypotheses for 41.2% of cases; its failures often begin from generic valid observations and add unsupported task-specific mechanisms.

Measure whether each proposed validation experiment would actually test its hypothesis. On the same 10-task, 17-component subset, have human annotators score validation plans from 0 for no meaningful validation, through 1 for indirect or incomplete validation, to 2 for a plan that fully tests the hypothesis, and aggregate with the lower annotator score. GPT-5.4 scores 1.71, Gemini-3.1-Pro 1.41, Claude-Sonnet-4.6 1.24, and Qwen-3-Coder 0.71. This rating evaluates the proposed experiment rather than whether the hypothesis itself is correct or whether the code executes successfully.

Identify what prevents validation plans from producing usable evidence. Cluster failed execute_python calls by error type for GPT-5.4, Claude-Sonnet-4.6, Gemini-3.1-Pro, and Qwen-3-Coder, using respectively 314, 101, 191, and 301 failed calls. The observed categories are Python or tensor-manipulation bugs, library or API misuse, runtime-environment errors, lookup errors, BOS or position-offset mistakes, and tool-protocol failures such as omitting the required result variable. These failures accompany code-execution success rates of 0.52 for GPT-5.4, 0.93 for Claude-Sonnet-4.6, 0.80 for Gemini-3.1-Pro, and 0.62 for Qwen-3-Coder.

Relate completed hypothesis validation to final explanation performance. Count components whose hypotheses are supported on the first, second, or third iteration and those still unresolved after the three-iteration budget. Claude-Sonnet-4.6 supports 106 components on the first hypothesis, 32 on the second, and 8 on the third, leaving 17 unresolved; GPT-5.4 supports 81, 26, and 18, leaving 38 unresolved; Qwen-3-Coder supports 65, 20, and 21, leaving 57 unresolved. Gemini-3.1-Pro lies between Claude-Sonnet-4.6 and GPT-5.4 in unresolved components. Claude-Sonnet-4.6 has the fewest unresolved components and the highest tag accuracy, while Qwen-3-Coder has the most unresolved components and the lowest final explanation scores among the tested systems.

Remove individual HYVE stages to test their contribution. On the full AGENTICINTERPBENCH, compare full HYVE with NO-OBSERVATION, which removes the dedicated observation stage but retains hypothesis generation and validation, and NO-VALIDATION, which sends the initial hypothesis directly to classification and summarization. For GPT-5.4, full/no-observation/no-validation scores are respectively 0.74/0.66/0.70 tag accuracy, 0.46/0.47/0.45 role quality, 0.63/0.59/0.60 task accuracy, and 0.52/0.52/0.52 execution success. For Claude-Sonnet-4.6 they are 0.79/0.72/0.73, 0.58/0.50/0.51, 0.75/0.57/0.65, and 0.93/0.94/0.94. For Gemini-3.1-Pro they are 0.76/0.73/0.69, 0.59/0.52/0.53, 0.83/0.73/0.69, and 0.80/0.61/0.80. For Qwen-3-Coder they are 0.67/0.65/0.68, 0.25/0.21/0.24, 0.25/0.23/0.24, and 0.62/0.46/0.85. Full HYVE has the highest task accuracy for every backbone and ablation comparison, with removal of either stage reducing task accuracy by 1–18 percentage points; it also has higher component-level scores in 14 of 16 comparisons.

Rule out that unrestricted tool access alone produces the same results as the structured workflow. Run HYVE and Claude Code with Claude-Sonnet-4.6 on the same 31-task subset containing 55 components and provide the same evaluation context, except that Claude Code is not required to follow HYVE’s staged workflow. HYVE obtains tag accuracy 0.811, role-description quality 0.639, task accuracy 0.767, and execution success 0.94, compared with Claude Code’s 0.770, 0.603, 0.767, and 0.69. Manual inspection finds that Claude Code performs a causal intervention in 15 of 31 cases, relies only on observational evidence in 12, and infers the task from examples without loading the model in 4.

Check that the reported backbone ordering is not produced by judge self-preference or a single stochastic run. Score role descriptions and task descriptions separately with GPT-5.4 and Gemini-3.1-Pro rather than only using their lower-score aggregate, and repeat runs on a fixed benchmark subset. Both judges give the same backbone ranking for task accuracy; for role-description quality, both place GPT-5.4 third and Qwen fourth, while Claude-Sonnet-4.6 and Gemini-3.1-Pro exchange the top two positions with only a small score difference. The authors report no consistent advantage for a judge’s own model family, and the repeated runs preserve the backbone-level trends.

Test whether the workflow transfers to a naturally trained language model circuit. Apply HYVE with GPT-5.4, Claude-Sonnet-4.6, and Gemini-3.1-Pro to the 10-component All-for-One circuit previously localized for three-operand A+B+C addition in Llama-3-8B. Construct component-level reference roles using targeted interventions and retain both causally necessary and causally redundant components, including operand-transfer attention heads, late-layer MLPs, and logit-lens-positive attention heads; have three human annotators independently rate each generated role note as correct, partial, or wrong and report the majority vote. GPT-5.4 produces 6 correct, 3 partially correct, and 1 wrong description; Claude-Sonnet-4.6 produces 8 correct, 2 partially correct, and 0 wrong; Gemini-3.1-Pro produces 1 correct, 2 partially correct, and 7 wrong. Claude-Sonnet-4.6 and GPT-5.4 recover the operand-transfer structure and distinguish necessary components from causally redundant late components, while Gemini-3.1-Pro frequently treats positional or logit-lens correlations as causal.
